This paper investigates Mutual Recognition of Conformity Assessment (MRCA), a
targeted mechanism distinct from broader Mutual Recognition Agreements (MRAs),
which streamlines regulatory compliance by enabling acceptance of product
evaluations (testing, inspection, certification) across jurisdictions. Using a
Poisson Pseudo-Maximum Likelihood (PPML) gravity model applied to bilateral
trade data (2010–2023) across 98 two-digit HS sectors, we find that MRCA
provisions are associated with an average 9.8% increase in exports, with
positive effects in 25 sectors (notably electrical machinery, machinery, and
dairy) and negative effects in seven (e.g., nickel, rail equipment).

## Key findings

- MRCA provisions raise exports by **9.8% on average**, with statistically
  significant gains in roughly one-third of sectors.
- The largest absolute gains are in high-value, technology-intensive
  industries: electrical machinery (HS85) and mechanical appliances (HS84) gain
  around **$25 million per country pair**.
- Dairy (HS04) and apparel (HS61) see export growth of **41–51%**.
- Resource-intensive sectors such as nickel, ores and railway locomotives see
  declines of **18–61%**, reflecting adjustment costs and greater competitive
  exposure.

## Policy implications

MRCA offers a practical, politically feasible route for UK–EU regulatory
cooperation that enhances market access without the legal and institutional
complexity of full alignment or treaty reform. Because gains are uneven, a
sector-sensitive approach is needed: prioritise industries with high
conformity costs and strong existing alignment — pharmaceuticals, electronics,
machinery — and use transitional arrangements or adjustment support where
competition bites. Beyond the EU, MRCA is a scalable template for UK
cooperation with CPTPP and Gulf Cooperation Council partners.

For the policy argument in brief, see
[After SPS: the EU trade barrier that needs fixing next](/blog/2026-09-14-after-sps-the-eu-trade-barrier-that-needs-fixing-next/index.qmd).
